notes.1: Many correct answers were seen. Candidates must ensure they read the question fully as several named the shapes square or triangle rather than the solid which was asked for. The most common incorrect answer was prism.
notes.2: Several candidates scored one of the two marks for naming two of the factors, usually 4 and 25. Few candidates named all four. Several candidates listed factors of 100 rather than factors which are square numbers.
notes.5: A large number of candidates did give the correct answer. Many candidates scored at least one mark for + y . one correct term, usually xy. Common errors were 2 x + xy and 2 x
notes.6: Only the more able candidates were successful with this question. Candidates need to understand how to attempt the first step of solving an equation. Several attempted to solve this by using trial and error.
notes.7: Many of the more able candidates gave the correct answer. Others clearly understood how to use a calculator correctly, but did not give the answer to 3 decimal places. Weaker candidates often appeared not to understand how to use their calculator. Candidates need to be familiar with their calculators and practice is clearly needed.
notes.8: This was generally well answered. The majority of candidates scored both marks.
notes.9: This question, being standard bookwork, resulted in a high number of candidates scoring full marks. Only a few weaker candidates misunderstood the question.
notes.10: Many candidates changed this question to decimals, while others gave 18 as their answer. The other 18 . 75 common incorrect answer was .
notes.11: In a small number of cases, errors or incomplete factorisations were seen in the answers of more able candidates. Less able candidates often gave a single term or omitted brackets.
notes.12: More able candidates were able to give the correct answer but a lot of uncertainty was evident in this question about what was required. The method mark was rarely given, but some did gain the special case mark for writing the fraction the wrong way around.
notes.13: More able candidates were able to give the correct answer. Other candidates often did not realise that there was already a common co-efficient and attempted to multiply one or both equations often incorrectly. Others attempted to solve the equations without eliminating one of the variables.
notes.14: Some candidates lost marks on this question as they gave a choice of answers for one or more parts.
notes.15: The formula for compound interest was often used successfully by more able candidates. Some worked out the 2 years separately. Candidates sometimes gave the interest as the answer rather than the total amount. Other candidates appeared not to be familiar with the concept of compound interest and many used the simple interest.
notes.16: Many candidates were successful in all parts of this question. There was some uncertainty about the two circle theorems applied.
notes.17: This question was very well answered suggesting basic order of operations is understood by the majority of candidates.
notes.19: Few candidates scored all 3 marks and there were many candidates who did not attempt this question. Many did not give an answer in the form directed, mx + c . A mark was lost often for the gradient of rather than − .
notes.21: This was well answered by most candidates. Some candidates tended to mix up the averages and the median was the least successful of the three. Some candidates did not show any working.
notes.general_comments: The majority of candidates showed a good level of knowledge and understanding and attempted all the questions. The majority of candidates showed working, but there were several cases where working needed to be shown and was not. The importance of showing working, in the working space below the question, must be stressed to all candidates.
notes.3a: This part was answered very well.
notes.3b: This part was also answered very well.
notes.4a: This part was generally correct. The most common incorrect answer was 35.
notes.4b: Although many candidates correctly answered this question it was not answered as well as part (a) . 7 was often seen, as was 34 from candidates using the noon temperature.
notes.14a: There was confusion about prime numbers with 27 being a common answer.
notes.14b: Several candidates did not appear to be familiar with irrational numbers.
notes.14c: Several candidates gave the answer in addition to 0.294.
notes.18a: The majority of candidates attempted the question, and there were many fully correct responses. However there appears to be confusion by a significant number about the order and signs of components of vectors.
notes.18b: This part was generally well answered. The most common error was giving the first sign as minus rather than plus. ⎛ 4 ⎞ ⎛ 2 ⎞ ⎜ ⎟ ⎜ ⎟ − 2 ⎝ ⎠ ⎝ ⎠
notes.20aii: This was generally well answered, although throughout some whole numbers for probabilities were seen in some answers.
notes.20aiii: This was a more challenging question, mainly due to candidates having to sort out both even numbers and factors. was a common wrong answer.
notes.20b: Some poor reading of the question was evident, since a denominator of 5 was very common. 4 2 2 5 5 4
notes.22a: The majority of candidates scored all 3 marks. Some weaker candidates understood the concept but did not draw straight lines between the points.
notes.22b: Time divided by speed was a common error and some used 25 minutes rather than 30 minutes in their correct (or incorrect) formula for the distance. Some answers were rather unrealistic.
